mainTopic: Can rules about danger (סכנה) be used to decide questions of prohibition (איסור)? A debate about how we handle uncertainty (ספק) in each area.
overview: A ברייתא says that if a snake bit a fig or melon and a bird or mouse later pecked it, we worry the new hole is right on the snake's hole, so the fruit is forbidden. רב הונא says you cannot learn איסור from this, because סכנה is different. רבא asks what the difference is, since uncertain איסור is also treated strictly. אביי points to a real difference: uncertain טומאה in רשות הרבים is טהור, while uncertain exposed water is forbidden. רבא answers that the טומאה leniency is a special tradition learned from סוטה, which applies only in רשות היחיד. רב שימי challenges him with a weasel carrying a שרץ over loaves of תרומה, where the doubt is also treated as טהור. The גמרא answers that this too comes from סוטה: the strict rule applies only to something that can be asked, and a weasel cannot. רב אשי then brings a ברייתא about a flask of purification water. Left open and found covered, it is טמאה. Left covered and found open, it is only פסולה. רבי יהושע בן לוי asks why, and the answer comes on the next amud.

steps.title: The fruit case: we worry the new hole is on top of the old one
steps.stepSummary: The last words of a ברייתא that was brought as a proof: we are concerned that the second hole was made exactly where the first (snake) hole was.
steps.simpleTranslation: We are concerned that perhaps it made its hole in the very place of the earlier hole.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a quote from a ברייתא that was brought as proof. The fruit had a snake's hole, a bird or mouse then pecked it, and we worry the peck landed right on the snake's hole.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the new hole might be covering up a snake's bite, we do not assume the fruit is safe. It stays forbidden. The person bringing this ברייתא wants to use this 'maybe it's in the same spot' worry to settle a question about איסור.

keyTerms.meaning: We are concerned, we take the possibility seriously

phrases.english: We are concerned that perhaps it perforated in the place of the hole.
phrases.notes: The bird or mouse may have pecked right where the snake bit, so the snake's venom could still be there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends a ברייתא brought as proof in the discussion before this section.
steps.raayaObject: That in a question of איסור we should also worry that a new hole landed on an old one.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא about a fig or melon pecked by a bird or mouse after a snake bit it.

steps.title: Danger is different from prohibition
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא rejects the proof: a danger case cannot teach us about an איסור case, because we are extra strict with danger.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Are you comparing a prohibition to danger? Danger is different!
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא pushes the proof away. The fruit case is about danger to life, and he says danger has its own rules.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof came from a סכנה case and was being used for an איסור case. רב הונא says we are stricter with possible danger than with possible prohibition, so being strict about the fruit tells us nothing about איסור.

keyTerms.meaning: A prohibition, something forbidden by הלכה

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two areas. The fruit is forbidden because it might be poisonous, which is סכנה. The question being proven is about איסור, something forbidden by הלכה. רב הונא's whole point is that these may follow different rules.

phrases.english: He said to him:
Are you comparing prohibition to danger?
Danger is different!

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי קָא מְדַמֵּית אִיסּוּרָא לְסַכַּנְתָּא? סַכָּנָה שָׁאנֵי
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from the fruit ברייתא.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It learns איסור from סכנה, even though danger is treated more strictly.

steps.title: רבא: both kinds of doubt are treated strictly anyway
steps.stepSummary: רבא questions the distinction: uncertain danger is treated strictly, but so is uncertain prohibition, so what difference is there?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: What is the difference? Doubtful danger is treated strictly? Doubtful prohibition is also treated strictly!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא challenges רב הונא's claim that danger is different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's point is that the rule for doubt is the same in both areas: when unsure, be strict. If so, the fruit case can still teach about איסור, and the proof stands.

phrases.english: Rava said to him: What is different?
Uncertain danger is treated stringently?
Uncertain prohibition is also treated stringently!

steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's claim that סכנה is different from איסור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both סְפֵק סכנה and סְפֵק איסור are treated strictly, so there is no real difference.

steps.title: אביי: impurity in public is lenient, exposed water is strict
steps.stepSummary: אביי shows a real difference: uncertain טומאה in a public place is treated as טהור, while uncertain exposed water is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: Is there really no difference between prohibition and danger? Look: uncertain impurity in a public place is pure, but uncertain exposed water is forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי pushes back against רבא with an example where doubt about an איסור-type matter is treated leniently, but doubt about danger is treated strictly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a person isn't sure whether he became טמא in רשות הרבים, he stays טהור, which is lenient. But if water may have been left uncovered, where a snake could have put venom in it, the water is forbidden, which is strict. So danger seems to get stricter treatment, and רב הונא's distinction is supported.

keyTerms.meaning: The public domain, a public place
Water left uncovered, which a snake may have drunk from and left venom in

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
And is there no difference between prohibition and danger?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא אִילּוּ סְפֵק טוּמְאָה בִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים –
phrases.english: But surely, uncertain impurity in the public domain —
its uncertain case is pure,
whereas uncertain exposed water is forbidden!
phrases.notes: The water was left uncovered, and even though we're not sure a snake actually drank from it, it's still off limits because of the danger.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא שָׁאנֵי בֵּין אִיסּוּרָא לְסַכַּנְתָּא? וְהָא אִילּוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's claim in step 3 and defends רב הונא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's claim that there is no difference between doubt about איסור and doubt about סכנה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Uncertain טומאה in a public place is lenient, while uncertain exposed water is strict, so danger is clearly treated differently.

steps.title: רבא: the impurity rule is a special tradition from סוטה
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the lenient rule for uncertain טומאה in public comes from a special tradition learned from סוטה, so it proves nothing about איסור in general.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: There, the rule is a tradition learned from סוטה. Just as a סוטה is forbidden only in a private place, so too טומאה from a doubt applies only in a private place.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers אביי. The טומאה case is a special exception with its own source, not a general rule about how to treat doubts about איסור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A סוטה becomes forbidden through a doubt only when she was secluded in a private place. From this we learn that doubtful טומאה makes something טמא only in רשות היחיד. Since this leniency comes from a special source, normal doubts about איסור are still treated strictly, just like danger.

keyTerms.meaning: They learned this rule as a tradition
A woman warned by her husband not to be alone with a certain man, who then was alone with him
The private domain, a private place

steps.whatToRemember: רבא holds that doubt about איסור and doubt about סכנה are both treated strictly. The lenient rule for uncertain טומאה in רשות הרבים is a special exception learned from סוטה, not proof that איסור is generally more lenient.

phrases.english: He said to him: There,
phrases.notes: "There" means the case of uncertain impurity in a public place that אביי just brought up.

phrases.english: they learned the halakha by tradition from sota,
just as a sota is in the private domain,
so too impurity is in the private domain.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the challenging case as a special exception with its own source.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The טומאה rule seemed to show that doubts about איסור are generally treated leniently, unlike danger.
steps.terutzMaskana: The leniency is a special rule learned from סוטה. Ordinary doubts about איסור are treated strictly, like danger.

steps.title: רב שימי's challenge from the weasel walking on loaves
steps.stepSummary: רב שימי shows a case of uncertain טומאה that is treated as טהור even without the public-place rule. Uncertain exposed water, by contrast, stays forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שימי objected: A dead creeping creature is in a weasel's mouth, and the weasel walks over loaves of תרומה. We are unsure whether the creature touched the loaves. In this case of doubt, the loaves are pure. But if we are unsure about exposed water, it is forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: רב שימי challenges רבא with another case where an uncertain טומאה is treated leniently. This case does not seem to depend on a public place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא said the lenient rule for uncertain טומאה only comes from a special סוטה tradition about public places. רב שימי finds a lenient טומאה case that does not mention a public place at all. So it looks like doubt in טומאה really is treated more leniently than doubt in danger, which brings back אביי's distinction.

keyTerms.meaning: A creeping creature. Its dead body makes things טמא.
Loaves of תרומה, holy food given to a כהן.
Unsure if it touched or did not touch.
Its doubt is treated as pure.

phrases.english: Rav Shimi raised an objection:
A dead creeping creature is in the mouth of a weasel,

phrases.aramaic: וְחוּלְדָּה מְהַלֶּכֶת עַל גַּבֵּי כִּכָּרוֹת שֶׁל תְּרוּמָה –
phrases.english: and the weasel is walking on top of loaves of terumah,
unsure if it touched, unsure if it did not touch,
its doubt is pure,
whereas doubtful exposed water is forbidden!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's answer in step 5 with a lenient טומאה case that does not depend on a public place.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's claim that the leniency for uncertain טומאה comes only from the סוטה tradition about public places.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The weasel case is lenient without any mention of a public place. So doubtful טומאה seems lenient in general, unlike doubtful danger.

steps.title: The weasel case also comes from סוטה: only something that can be asked
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the weasel case is also learned from סוטה. Just as a סוטה can be asked what happened, the strict rule applies only to something that has awareness to be asked.
steps.simpleTranslation: There too, the הלכה is learned from סוטה. A סוטה is someone who has the awareness to be asked. So here too, the rule applies only to something that has the awareness to be asked.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבא by showing that the weasel case also comes from the special סוטה tradition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The סוטה tradition teaches two limits. Doubtful טומאה is strict only in a private place, and only when the doubt involves something that can be asked, like a person. A weasel cannot be asked, so its doubt is lenient because of the סוטה tradition, not because איסור is generally lenient. So the weasel case gives no proof that danger is stricter than איסור.

keyTerms.meaning: Something with enough awareness to be asked about what happened.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the loaves are pure because a weasel is less likely to touch them. They are pure only because a weasel cannot be asked, so the strict סוטה rule does not apply.

phrases.english: There too,
they learned the halacha from sotah:

phrases.aramaic: מָה סוֹטָה דָּבָר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ דַּעַת לִישָּׁאֵל,
phrases.english: just as a sotah is something that has the awareness to be asked,

phrases.aramaic: אַף הָכָא נָמֵי דָּבָר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ דַּעַת לִישָּׁאֵל.
phrases.english: so too here, it must be something that has the awareness to be asked.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם נָמֵי הִלְכְתָא גְּמִירִי לַהּ מִסּוֹטָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב שימי's challenge from step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Brings the challenging case under the same special source (סוטה) already used in step 5.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The weasel case shows that doubtful טומאה is lenient in general, unlike danger.
steps.terutzMaskana: The weasel case is lenient only because the סוטה tradition limits the strict rule to things that can be asked. So it proves nothing about איסור in general.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a key rule of doubtful טומאה: the strict rule applies only in a private place, and only when the doubt involves something that can be asked.

steps.title: רב אשי's proof: a flask left open and found covered is טמא
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי opens a new proof from a ברייתא. A flask left open and later found covered is טמא, because we assume a טמא person came in and covered it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Come and hear. If someone left a flask open, then came back and found it covered, it is טמא. This is because I say a טמא person came in there and covered it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי starts a new proof about whether danger is stricter than טומאה. This first part of the ברייתא sets up the contrast he will draw next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone clearly covered the flask while the owner was away, so the ברייתא assumes a טמא person came in and covered it, and it rules the flask טמאה. This first case sets up the contrast with the second case, where the flask is found uncovered.

keyTerms.meaning: "For I say": we assume this is what happened.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said: Come and hear:
A flask that he left uncovered
phrases.notes: This is a flask of purification water, the kind used for sprinkling.

phrases.english: and he came and found it covered is impure,
for I say:
phrases.notes: תוספות point out that this is a ברייתא. The משנה in פרה has the same flask case, but it calls the first case פסולה and never says 'שאני אומר'. That line is exactly what רב אשי needs, which is why he quotes the ברייתא.

phrases.english: An impure person went in there and covered it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the רב שימי exchange ends, רב אשי brings a fresh source on the main question of steps 2-3.
steps.raayaObject: That doubtful danger is treated more strictly than doubtful טומאה or איסור. This supports אביי's distinction (and רב הונא's 'סכנה שאני') against רבא.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A משנה about a flask of water that was left uncovered or covered.

steps.title: The flask left covered and found open is only disqualified
steps.stepSummary: The second half of the ברייתא: a flask left covered and found open, where a weasel, snake, or dew could have gotten in, is פסולה (disqualified).
steps.simpleTranslation: If he left it covered and came back and found it open, it is disqualified if a weasel could drink from it, or a snake according to רבן גמליאל, or if dew could have fallen into it at night.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting רב אשי's ברייתא. The point of the proof will be drawn out in the coming lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the ברייתא only worries that a weasel, a snake, or dew got into the water, and it does not suspect a טמא person. So the water is called פסולה (disqualified for sprinkling), not טמאה. This difference from the first case sets up the contrast רב אשי is building.

keyTerms.meaning: Disqualified for use, but not called טמאה.

phrases.english: If he left it covered
and came back and found it uncovered,
if a weasel could drink from it,
or a snake, according to Rabban Gamliel,
or if dew fell into it at night,
it is disqualified.
phrases.notes: Notice the word: it says disqualified, not impure. That difference matters for the proof.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same משנה with the opposite case: left covered, found uncovered.
steps.raayaObject: Whether danger is treated more strictly than doubtful טומאה or איסור.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The second clause of the flask משנה, where the water is only called פסולה.

steps.title: Why don't we suspect a טמא person opened the flask?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי asks why the second case of the ברייתא is only פסולה, with no worry that a טמא person opened the flask.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהושע בן לוי said: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע בן לוי asks a short question about the second half of the ברייתא. The גמרא is setting up the next move, and his answer comes at the start of the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first case, a flask left open and found covered is טמאה, because we assume a טמא person came in and covered it. So in the second case, a flask left covered and found open, we might expect the same worry: a טמא person came in and uncovered it. The question is why the ברייתא only worries about a weasel, snake, or dew, and only calls the flask פסולה.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason? A request to explain the logic behind a ruling.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two cases of the ברייתא. Open then found covered is טמאה, because a person did the covering. Covered then found open is only פסולה. רבי יהושע בן לוי is asking about the second case.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
What is the reason?
phrases.notes: He means: why is the flask only פסולה in the second case, with no worry that a טמא person opened it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי: מָה טַעַם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the ruling quoted in step 9, compared against the case in step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the משנה does not suspect a טמא person of uncovering the flask, when in the first case it does suspect a טמא person of covering it.
